SEC26A-01.note: 'The young' (of earlier broods) is a plural noun, so 'are'; the begging belongs to the nestlings, so 'their'. 'is' attracts readers who take 'young' as singular; 'its' attracts toward 'nest'.

SEC26A-02.note: 'Each' takes singular 'was'; 'when the sponsor put' fixes past progressive. 'were keeping' attracts via 'patients/wards'; 'is keeping' via the present-tense frame sentences.

SEC26A-03.note: Restrictive participle: many trays exist, so 'kept nearest the door' identifies which one and takes no comma. B (nonrestrictive comma) is the strongest; D's comma between participle and its complement is struck on sight.

SEC26A-04.note: 'since ... last spring' requires present perfect; singular 'ointment' requires 'has'. 'have been' attracts via 'clinics'; 'was prescribed' via the past-tense 'voted'.

SEC26A-05.note: 'needles' is plural (are) and the agent is 'bacteria' (plural, them). 'it' attracts toward 'pine'; 'is' toward 'pine' as nearest noun; readers treating 'bacteria' as singular pick B.

SEC26A-06.note: Plural 'oats', past study frame ('studied', 'credited'), and 'seldom ... rotten enough' needs a copula, so 'were'. 'has/have seldom ... rotten' lacks a participle and reads wrong; 'was' is the live trap.

SEC26A-07.note: Two independent clauses; the second ('the tough cord ... had a second ... market') adds a new point, not an elaboration, so a period. The comma garden-paths 'the tough cord' as an appositive to 'catgut', leaving 'had' subjectless; the colon is the strongest distractor (some readers would accept it since the clause partly describes catgut).

SEC26A-08.note: 'pancreas' is singular despite the -s and 'mice'; the generic present ('unless the animals receive') rules out past. 'are damaged' attracts via 'mice'; 'was damaged' via the past 'went on'.

SEC26A-09.note: Plural possessive: the harvest of the cooperative's growers collectively, contrasted with the founder's own trees. 'grower's' is strongest (founder/one grower); 'growers' without apostrophe and 'grower' are struck as non-possessive.

SEC26A-10.note: Intransitive 'spray' ends the introductory clause; 'the vines growing ...' is the main-clause subject of 'were showing'. A/B garden-path 'the vines' as object of 'spray', stranding 'were showing'; D's semicolon after a dependent clause.

SEC26B-01.note: Plural 'engineers' takes 'have'; the reconstructed thing is the single status report, so 'it'. 'them' attracts toward 'stations'/'dishes'; 'has' toward 'recording'/'dish'.

SEC26B-02.note: Singular 'front'; habitual present matching 'whenever ... lakes ... drain'. 'were/are prone' attract via 'crevasses'/'currents'; 'was prone' via the past-tense study frame.

SEC26B-03.note: Independent clause boundary; the sentence already uses a colon to list the two defects, so a second colon is out and the semicolon is right. Comma = splice, no mark = run-on; the colon is attractive because the second clause elaborates on the line.

SEC26B-04.note: Plural 'segments'; a specific past time ('on the evening of the ... open house') takes simple past, not present perfect. 'has/was' attract via 'mirror'/'dome'; 'have been cleaned' via the present-tense result sentence.

SEC26B-05.note: Elliptical 'do [lengthen]' with plural 'tapes'; the elided verb is 'lengthens', which 'were' cannot stand in for, and steel's expansion is a standing physical fact. 'were' is strongly attractive because of 'nineteenth-century' and the past 'corrected'; 'was/does' are singular.

SEC26B-06.note: Singular 'receiver' takes 'is'; it tracks the grains (plural), so 'them'. 'it' attracts toward the singular 'atmosphere'/'telescope'; 'are' attracts via 'domes'.

SEC26B-07.note: Transitive 'blasted the ridge' closes the introductory clause; 'loosened boulders ...' is the main subject of 'fell'. A (comma before 'the ridge') makes 'the ridge loosened boulders ... fell' ungrammatical; B is a run-on garden path; C semicolon after a dependent clause. Mirror image of A-10.

SEC26B-08.note: Plural 'staves'; 'while the ... bricks ... slowly cooled' sets past progressive. 'was being' attracts via 'wall'/'hearth'; 'are being' via the present 'is relined'.

SEC26B-09.note: Single-bunk hut and every page 'signed in the same hand' imply one observer, so singular possessive. 'observers'' is strongest (summer visitors); 'observers'/'observer' are non-possessive before 'sketches'.

SEC26B-10.note: Series items contain internal commas ('a dust counter ...; and a narrow-angle camera, the heaviest ...'), and the later semicolon fixes the separator, so a semicolon. The comma is the trap; colon and no mark are struck.

SEC26C-01.note: Singular 'curtain' takes 'was'; the neglect was by the three painters, so 'them'. 'were' attracts via 'painters'/'backdrops'; 'it' toward 'loft'/'stage'.

SEC26C-02.note: 'The illiterate' (adjective as noun) is plural; 'since a ... archivist discarded' requires present perfect. 'has been' is the strong trap for readers treating 'the illiterate' as singular; 'was/were' fail the 'since' tense.

SEC26C-03.note: Plural 'copes'; a specific past event ('on the eve of the great fire ... and carried'). 'is/are removed' attract via the inventory's present 'notes'/'is worn'; 'was' via 'inventory'.

SEC26C-04.note: Independent clause followed by a clause that explains the clue, so a colon. Comma = splice; no mark = run-on; 'sight the,' is garbled.

SEC26C-05.note: Plural 'copyists'; interrupted action ('when floodwaters ... spread') takes past progressive. 'was decorating' attracts via 'scriptorium'; 'have/has decorated' via present-perfect habit.

SEC26C-06.note: Singular 'editor' takes 'was'; he revised the novel (its final chapter), so 'it'. 'them' attracts toward 'sonnets'/'letters'; 'were' toward 'sonnets'.

SEC26C-07.note: Singular 'toll'; specific past event ('at the funeral of the bell's first patron'). 'is audible' attracts via the present 'still hangs'; plurals via 'shepherds/hills'.
SEC26C-07.drop_reason: Too easy for the hard route: a singular subject and an explicit one-time past occasion decide it at a glance.

SEC26C-08.note: Singular 'restorer'; 'before the councillors quit paying' sets a past-progressive frame. 'have/were' attract via 'paintings'; 'has been cleaning' fails the completed past.

SEC26C-09.note: He had one letter book ('that one volume'), so the participle is nonrestrictive and takes a comma. The restrictive no-comma reading (B) is the strongest distractor; 'book filled,' is struck on sight. Inverse of A-03.

SEC26C-10.convention: 'cast' is also a simple past form, so a generic singular 'the apprentice cast ...' agrees with the past-tense 'set'/'pulled' in the same sentence; only the content of the final sentence ('three or four boys') prefers the plural
SEC26C-10.note: Plural nonpossessive subject; the guild records sentence implies several apprentices. Possessives C/D leave no subject; B is grammatical because 'cast' is an unmarked past tense, so number is decided by content, not by a convention.
SEC26C-10.drop_reason: Number is decided by content, not convention: 'cast' is an unmarked past tense, so the generic singular 'the apprentice cast' is grammatical (the authored explanation concedes this), leaving a second defensible option.

SEC26D-01.note: Singular 'diner' takes 'judges'; what is judged is the one precise price ('it'), contrasted with 'the rounded prices'. 'them' attracts toward 'prices'.

SEC26D-02.note: Singular 'Bilingualism'; specific past ('at the height of the harbor's grain trade'). 'were' attracts via 'vendors'; 'has been' via the present-perfect 'has shaped'.
SEC26D-02.drop_reason: Too easy for the hard route: a singular abstract subject and an explicit finished past period ('at the height of', 'collapsed') decide it at a glance.

SEC26D-03.note: The dash opens a pair that the comma after 'Sentinel' does not close, so B fails; semicolon and 'newspaper the,' are struck. Note: the town had one paper, so ideal punctuation would be paired commas; the close-appositive A is acceptable but the batch has no fully nonrestrictive option.

SEC26D-04.note: Plural 'tenants'; the habitual present ('as long as that increase stays') sets present. 'were accepting' attracts via the parenthetical 'found'; 'is' via 'building'.

SEC26D-05.note: Singular 'study'; 'since that first recruitment drive' requires present perfect. 'have been following' attracts via 'interns'/'classmates'.

SEC26D-06.note: Singular 'suffix'; the verb 'disappeared' needs perfect 'has', since 'is/are ... disappeared' is non-standard. 'have never' attracts via 'verbs'.

SEC26D-07.note: Plural 'teams' takes 'have'; the wording belongs to the questionnaire, so 'its'. 'their' attracts toward 'teams'/'villages'; 'has' toward 'questionnaire'/'office'.

SEC26D-08.note: Plural 'volunteers'; 'since the school's closure' requires present perfect. 'has coached' attracts via 'grant'/'desk'.

SEC26D-09.convention: a colon after a complete independent clause may introduce an appositive that identifies or renames the preceding noun
SEC26D-09.note: End-of-sentence appositive renaming 'Ursula Wexler' takes a comma. Semicolon makes a fragment; no mark runs the name into the description; the colon is defensible because the clause before it is complete.
SEC26D-09.drop_reason: The colon is defensible before a sentence-final appositive after a complete clause, and the passage itself has a misplaced modifier ('foreman trained ... by her own father' reads as the foreman being trained), which a conventions item should not carry.

SEC26D-10.note: Lone appointee, and the verb 'rules' is singular, so plain singular noun. Possessives leave 'rules' as a noun and the clause without a verb; 'parliamentarians' clashes with 'rules'.

tells: The dash is never the key: it appears only as an unpaired/mismatched distractor (SEC26A-03 C, SEC26D-03 B).
Trailing-comma options ('tray kept,', 'book filled,') and the garbled 'X the,' shape always lose (SEC26A-03 D, SEC26C-09 D, SEC26C-04 D, SEC26D-03 D).

A semicolon after an introductory 'Before/As ...' clause always loses (SEC26A-10 D, SEC26B-07 C); the semicolon wins only in the internal-comma series (SEC26B-10) and the second-colon item (SEC26B-03).

In the 2x2 verb-pronoun items, the pronoun key never refers to the nearest noun before the blank (SEC26A-05, SEC26B-01, SEC26B-06, SEC26C-01, SEC26C-06, SEC26D-07); a test-taker can reject the pronoun that matches the nearest noun.

Tense items are decided by a single cue that is always present: 'since' -> present perfect (SEC26A-04, SEC26C-02, SEC26D-05, SEC26D-08); a dated past event -> simple past (SEC26B-04, SEC26C-03, SEC26C-07, SEC26D-02). That is the rule, but the cue word is very visible.
Letter spread and number of the key look balanced; I found no letter tell.
